procedural_history.originating_court: Special Judge, Prevention of Corruption Act, Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 24.07.2017 of the High Court of M.P. Principal Seat at Jabalpur in CRR No. 515 of 2017.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur heard CRR No. 515 of 2017 and issued a judgment and order on 24.07.2017. An appeal against the order dated 17th November, 2017 passed by the Special Judge, Prevention of Corruption Act, Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh in Sessions Trial No.573 of 2014 was pending before the High Court of Madhya Pradesh.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The accused appellant appealed to the Supreme Court, challenging the High Court's judgment and order dated 24.07.2017. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashing the prosecution and setting aside the order of the Special Judge. The Supreme Court also closed the appeal pending before the High Court.

directions: Quash the impugned prosecution/proceedings registered and numbered as Sessions Session Trial No.573 of 2014.

The appeal pending before the High Court against the order dated 17th November, 2017 passed by the learned Special Judge, Prevention of Corruption Act, Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh in Sessions Trial No.573 of 2014 shall also stand closed.
Bail bond, if any shall stand discharged accordingly.

issue.issue_text: Whether the initiation of the prosecution against the appellant was tenable in law.

facts: The appellant was prosecuted for defamation (Section 500 IPC) for statements made against the Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh.
The prosecution was initiated by the Public Prosecutor under Section 199(2) of the Cr.P.C.
The State Government granted sanction to the Public Prosecutor to file the complaint on June 24, 2014.
The Public Prosecutor filed the complaint on the very same day the sanction was granted.
During cross-examination in the trial, the Public Prosecutor admitted that he had not scrutinized the materials and had filed the complaint on the orders of the State Government.
law: For a prosecution under Section 199(2) Cr.P.C., the Public Prosecutor must independently apply their mind to the materials of the case before filing a complaint.
The Public Prosecutor cannot act merely as a post office or on the dictates of the government; they must form their own independent judgment about whether a prosecution is warranted.
application: The Court found two key pieces of evidence showing the Public Prosecutor had not applied his mind.
First, the Public Prosecutor explicitly admitted during cross-examination that he did not scrutinize the materials and filed the complaint simply because the State Government ordered him to do so.

Second, the Court noted the "haste" with which the complaint was filed—on the very same day the government granted sanction. This haste served as prima facie evidence that the prosecutor likely did not have time to properly review the materials and apply his mind.
Based on these factors, the Court determined that the Public Prosecutor had failed in his legal duty to exercise independent judgment.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the prosecution, finding its very initiation to be untenable in law. The decision was based on the failure of the Public Prosecutor to independently apply his mind before filing the complaint. This failure was established by the prosecutor's own admission that he acted on government orders without scrutinizing the materials, a conclusion further supported by the extreme haste with which the complaint was filed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction and sentence of the appellant can be sustained when the very initiation of the prosecution is found to be untenable in law.

facts: The appellant was accused of making defamatory statements against the Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh.
The State Government sanctioned the Public Prosecutor (PP) to file a criminal complaint for defamation under a special procedure (Section 199(2) Cr.P.C.).
The PP filed the complaint on the very same day the sanction was granted.
During the trial, the PP admitted in cross-examination that he had not scrutinized the materials and had filed the complaint on the orders of the State Government.
Despite this, the appellant was convicted by the trial court, and an appeal was pending in the High Court.
law: Section 199(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) provides a special procedure for prosecuting defamation against high public functionaries.
This procedure can only be used if the defamatory statements have a reasonable connection to the discharge of the person's public duties.

A Public Prosecutor filing a complaint under this section must independently apply their mind to the materials to be satisfied that an offence has been committed. They cannot act mechanically on the orders of the government.
Article 142 of the Constitution grants the Supreme Court extraordinary power to pass any order necessary to do complete justice.
application: The Court found that the prosecution was untenable from its very beginning for two main reasons.

First, the Court examined the alleged defamatory statements and concluded they had no reasonable connection with the Chief Minister's discharge of his public duties. Therefore, the special procedure under Section 199(2) Cr.P.C. should not have been used in the first place.

Second, the Court noted the PP's admission that he had not scrutinized the case materials and had simply acted on the government's orders. The haste with which the complaint was filed (on the same day as the sanction) further indicated a lack of independent application of mind. This failure by the PP made the initiation of the complaint legally invalid.

The Court reasoned that if the very foundation of the prosecution is illegal, then everything that follows, including the trial and conviction, has no legal basis ("would not have any legs to stand").
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the conviction and sentence could not be sustained because the very initiation of the prosecution was fundamentally flawed and untenable in law. Since the legal basis for the case was invalid from the start, the resulting conviction was also invalid. The Court invoked its special powers under Article 142 to quash the entire proceedings, setting aside the conviction and sentence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the fact that the trial has concluded in a conviction and an appeal is pending before the High Court should prevent the quashing of the prosecution on the grounds of it being untenable in law from its inception.

facts: A criminal prosecution for defamation was initiated against the appellant under a special procedure (Section 199(2) Cr.P.C.).
The trial concluded, and the appellant was convicted and sentenced.
An appeal against this conviction was pending before the High Court when the Supreme Court heard the case.
The appellant challenged the very initiation and maintainability of the prosecution itself.
law: A prosecution under the special procedure of Section 199(2) Cr.P.C. is only permissible if the alleged defamatory statements have a reasonable connection with the discharge of the public official's duties.

A Public Prosecutor filing a complaint under this section must independently scrutinize the materials and be satisfied that an offence is disclosed, rather than simply acting on the orders of the government.
The Supreme Court can use its special and extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 142 of the Constitution to ensure complete justice.
application: The Court first determined that the prosecution was fundamentally flawed and "untenable in law" from its inception.
It found that the appellant's statements had no reasonable connection to the Chief Minister's public duties, making the special prosecution procedure unavailable.
It also found that the Public Prosecutor had improperly filed the complaint on the orders of the State Government without applying his own mind.
Based on these fundamental flaws, the Court reasoned that the subsequent conviction and pending appeal were irrelevant and should not prevent it from intervening.

The Court stated, "Merely because the trial is over and has ended in the conviction of the appellant and the matter is presently pending before the High Court in appeal should not come in the way of our interdicting the same."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the idea that a conviction and pending appeal should bar it from quashing the case. It held that since the very initiation of the prosecution was legally invalid, the "requirements of justice" demanded that the Court use its special powers under Article 142 to carry its conclusion to its "logical end." Consequently, it quashed the entire prosecution, set aside the conviction, and closed the pending appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the initiation of the prosecution against the appellant was tenable in law.
appellant_arguments: The prosecution was not tenable because the Public Prosecutor failed to apply his mind independently and did not scrutinize the materials before filing the complaint.
The Public Prosecutor admitted in cross-examination that he filed the complaint solely on the orders of the State Government.
The allegedly defamatory statements, for which sanction was granted, had no reasonable nexus with the discharge of public duties by the concerned minister.
respondent_arguments: The prosecution was validly initiated through the Public Prosecutor as per the procedure laid out in Section 199(2) of the Cr.P.C.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction and sentence of the appellant can be sustained when the very initiation of the prosecution is found to be untenable in law.
appellant_arguments: If the initiation of the prosecution itself is untenable and illegal, then the subsequent conviction and sentence based on that prosecution are void and cannot be sustained.
respondent_arguments: The conviction was the result of a full trial where evidence was presented and should stand on its own merits, irrespective of any initial procedural issues.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the fact that the trial has concluded in a conviction and an appeal is pending before the High Court should prevent the quashing of the prosecution on the grounds of it being untenable in law from its inception.
appellant_arguments: A fundamental defect like an untenable initiation of prosecution is not cured by the conclusion of the trial and should be quashed at any stage, even if an appeal against conviction is pending.
respondent_arguments: The appropriate remedy for the appellant is to challenge the conviction on its merits in the pending appeal before the High Court, not to seek the quashing of the entire prosecution at this late stage.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: If the very initiation of a prosecution is untenable in law, any subsequent conviction and sentence resulting from it are invalid and cannot stand, regardless of the trial having been completed or an appeal being pending.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found the very initiation of the prosecution to be untenable in law and not maintainable on its face. This was because the Public Prosecutor failed to independently apply his mind, as evidenced by the haste with which the complaint was filed on the same day sanction was granted. Furthermore, the allegedly defamatory statements made by the appellant lacked a reasonable nexus with the discharge of the public official's duties, a necessary condition for such a prosecution.
legal_tests_applied: To determine if an act falls within the discharge of official duties, there must be a 'direct and reasonable nexus between the nature of the duties cast upon the public servant and the act constituting an offence'. Simply being a public servant is not enough; a reasonable connection between the duties and the alleged act is required.

A Public Prosecutor filing a complaint under Section 199(2) Cr.P.C. must independently apply their mind and have 'due satisfaction' that the materials disclose an offence against a public functionary that adversely affects the interests of the State. Filing a complaint without this independent scrutiny is a failure of the prosecutor's duty to the court and the collective.
policy_considerations: The 'requirements of justice' demand that a prosecution found to be untenable from its inception should be quashed, and the Court will use its special and extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 142 to do so, even if the trial has already concluded in a conviction and an appeal is pending.

A Public Prosecutor has a lawful obligation under the Code and a duty to both the court and the collective. They cannot act merely on the orders of the government but must independently scrutinize the case materials before initiating a prosecution.
